interest: This file provides a valuable window into the early economic administration of the Allied Occupation of Japan, specifically illustrating how agricultural commodities were managed to balance occupation financing, domestic industry demands, and international allocations. It documents the deliberate U.S. strategy of utilizing state-trading monopolies (the U.S. Commercial Company and SCAP) to capture export foreign exchange to offset food relief expenditures and protect Japanese assets from Allied reparations claims. Furthermore, it reveals the contentious friction between the U.S. government bureaucracy and private American commercial merchants, highlighting the frustration of prewar tea traders over excluded private commerce, bureaucratic inertia, and the poor quality of government-supervised shipments.
keywords: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP)
overview: This file comprises State Department correspondence, memoranda, and industry petitions from October 1945 to July 1947 (decimal file 894.61332) concerning the resumption, regulation, and international allocation of Japanese tea exports during the Allied Occupation of Japan. It details early postwar economic planning involving the State Department's Commodities, International Resources, and Japanese and Korean Economic divisions, alongside the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP), the U.S. Commercial Company (USCC), and the Combined Food Board (CFB). The documents illuminate the U.S. policy of maintaining a government-to-government monopoly over Japanese tea exports to generate vital foreign exchange for financing Japanese food relief imports and to prevent other Allied nations from absorbing exports into reparations accounts. The collection also captures vigorous lobbying by the American tea trade, led by the Tea Association of the U.S.A., which pressed for technical supervision over tea quality, opposed British procurement preferences, and protested SCAP's continuing exclusion of private American tea merchants in favor of state-controlled trade for the 1946 and 1947 crops.

subfiles.about: Reports on plans for the U.S. Commercial Company to become the exclusive buyer of exportable Japanese tea to secure foreign exchange and addresses upcoming Combined Food Board allocations.
subfiles.from: Mrs. Moffat (Mary A. Moffat), Commodities Division, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Moffat informs Mr. Sellon of discussions with Edwin Martin regarding plans for the U.S. Commercial Company (USCC) to purchase all exportable Japanese tea and other products for the next six months to a year. This arrangement is designed to accrue foreign exchange to offset expected U.S. food supplies to Japan and prevent other Allied powers from demanding exports as reparations. She stresses the necessity of establishing a formal U.S. policy position before the upcoming Combined Food Board tea allocation meeting in mid-November and notes ongoing coordination with Merrill Gay of the Division of Commercial Policy.
subfiles.title: Office Memorandum from Mrs. Moffat to Mr. Sellon on Japanese Tea
subfiles.to: Mr. Sellon (John A. Sellon), Commodities Division, Department of State

subfiles.about: Summarizes a telephone discussion between Sellon and Whitman regarding Japanese export tea availability, Far Eastern Commission reorganization, and coordination with the Combined Food Board.
subfiles.from: Mr. Sellon (John A. Sellon), International Resources Division, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Sellon and Whitman discuss conflicting cables from Japan regarding available export tea, with one citing zero exportable quality and another estimating 3,000,000 pounds. Whitman reports that following the admission of Russian members to the Far Eastern Commission, the JK division will propose an Inter-Allied Committee to coordinate tea exports with the Combined Food Board Tea Committee to maximize useful foreign exchange. The memorandum also details procedures for USCC procurement and distribution to U.S. importers, and notes U.S. opposition to British proposals extending exclusive purchasing controls to non-Napier sources like Japan.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Telephone Conversation between Mr. Sellon and Mr. Whitman on Japanese Tea Export and CFB Allocation

subfiles.about: Informs the Tea Association that the U.S. Commercial Company manages marketing details for Japanese tea and confirms that occupation authorities prioritize tea exports.
subfiles.from: Edward G. Cale, Associate Chief, International Resources Division, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Cale acknowledges Mitchell's inquiry of May 3 regarding the availability, shipment, and handling of new crop Japanese teas. He explains that the U.S. Commercial Company is in closer touch with operating details and that USCC representative William Trout has already shared available information. Cale emphasizes that occupation authorities consider tea an important export commodity receiving special marketing attention, and he promises to keep the Tea Association updated as further details develop.
subfiles.title: Letter from Edward G. Cale to George F. Mitchell regarding Japanese Tea Availability
subfiles.to: George F. Mitchell, President, Tea Association of the United States of America

subfiles.about: Requests comprehensive details from the State Department and USCC on the handling, volume, and quality control of the upcoming Japanese tea crop.
subfiles.from: George F. Mitchell, President, Tea Association of the United States of America
subfiles.summary: Writing pursuant to a resolution passed by the Tea Association's Board of Directors, Mitchell inquires about forthcoming shipments of new crop Japanese teas to the United States. He asks for particulars regarding estimated export volumes, types of tea, and whether trade will be handled through former exporters in Japan. Mitchell stresses that the American market requires specific tea types and urges that qualified experts supervise shipments in Japan to prevent the delivery of unsatisfactory goods.
subfiles.title: Letter from George F. Mitchell to Edward G. Cale on Handling the New Crop of Japanese Teas
subfiles.to: Edward G. Cale (addressed as Mr. Cole), Department of State

subfiles.about: Announces the establishment of the Japan Tea Committee to assist U.S. government authorities in arranging the importation and distribution of Japanese tea.
subfiles.from: Duncan J. MacKenzie, Chairman, Japan Tea Committee, Tea Association of the U.S.A.
subfiles.summary: MacKenzie notifies the Secretary of State that the Tea Association of the U.S.A. has appointed a special Japan Tea Committee to cooperate with government agencies on tea shipments arriving through SCAP. He lists committee members Arthur T. Hellyer, E. W. Payne, Vere Brown, and himself, citing their extensive commercial experience in Japan and the Far East, including his own leadership of the Shizuoka Tea Exporters Association. The committee offers its expertise to help government authorities coordinate the technical details of importing and distributing Japanese tea to the domestic trade.
subfiles.title: Letter from D. J. MacKenzie to the Secretary of State offering Cooperation of the Japan Tea Committee
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State (James F. Byrnes)

subfiles.about: Protests SCAP's decision to permit 400 private commercial traders into Japan while continuing state monopoly controls and excluding former American tea exporters.
subfiles.from: Duncan J. MacKenzie, Chairman, Japan Tea Committee, Tea Association of the U.S.A.
subfiles.summary: The letter conveys the dismay of the American tea trade following a press release from Tokyo announcing that 400 private trade representatives will be permitted into Japan after August 15, 1947, while former American tea exporters remain excluded and the 1947 crop remains under SCAP and USCC control. It highlights months of unsuccessful appeals by the Tea Association of the U.S.A. and Western States Tea Association to assign a qualified American technical tea expert to SCAP to rectify defects seen in the 1946 shipments. The Association protests this policy as discriminatory against the tea trade and calls for prompt corrective action.
subfiles.title: Letter from the Tea Association of the U.S.A. protesting Exclusion of American Tea Exporters from Japan
subfiles.to: Director of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Explains why the 1947 Japanese tea crop must remain under government-to-government trade controls rather than private commercial channels.
subfiles.from: Roswell M. Whitman, Associate Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
keywords: Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.summary: Whitman responds to MacKenzie's protest, assuring him that the government does not intend to discriminate against American tea exporters. He explains that private traders are not permitted to enter Japan before August 15, 1947, or execute contracts before September 1, whereas the 1947 tea crop is harvested and ready for shipment in July, necessitating continuation of state-directed trade under SCAP and USCC. He notes that major commodities like raw silk and cotton textiles are likewise restricted from private trade, and reassures the industry that government controls will be dismantled as quickly as conditions allow.
subfiles.title: Letter from Roswell M. Whitman to D. J. MacKenzie defending Government Controls on 1947 Tea Crop
subfiles.to: Duncan J. MacKenzie, Chairman, Japan Tea Committee, Tea Association of the U.S.A.
